entries.answer_en: I have two sides. I build AI systems, and I can also run a project. I work hands-on with LLMs, RAG, Python, and APIs. And I can talk to the people who pay for it, set a timeline, and deliver. I have done that in education and in payment systems.
entries.followup_en: In seven years of government payments, a wrong action was worse than a slow one. So I put checks in AI work too: a person reviews important output, and we keep a log. Simple tools help because they are easier to test and explain. If I only studied a tool, I say that. I do not pretend production experience I do not have.
entries.answer_ar: لدي مزيج قوي من المهارات التقنية في الذكاء الاصطناعي وخبرة إدارة المشاريع. أستطيع بناء حلول الذكاء الاصطناعي وإدارة أصحاب المصلحة والجداول الزمنية والتسليم. أنا عملي في LLMs و RAG و Python و APIs، ولدي سجل حافل في تسليم المشاريع في التعليم وأنظمة الدفع.

I am interested in in-country models because the data cannot leave. That is a real engineering problem, not a demo. I also want generative AI to be the main work, not a side project.

entries.answer_en: The BTEC similarity checker at the Ministry of Education. Review used to mean reading everything by hand. Now teachers get a short list of flagged cases, with the two texts side by side. I am proud that they trusted it, because it never accused a student. It only showed the evidence, and the teacher decided.
entries.followup_en: This is not an LLM system. It uses embeddings, chunking, and cosine similarity, then shows both passages. Teachers used to spend a long time reading every assignment. After we tuned the threshold with them on real cases, they reviewed a short list instead. Trust came from the design: the tool flags, a person decides. That is the result I am proud of, not a fancy model.
entries.answer_ar: أفخر بفاحص التشابه في BTEC: قلّل المراجعة اليدوية، ولم يتهم الطالب، والمعلم هو من يقرر.

entries.answer_en: In the early-warning project, my first version looked strong on paper, then failed in real use. The problem was data leakage. I scaled before the split, and a random split let later terms leak into earlier ones. The score was fake. I put every step in a Scikit-learn Pipeline and split by time.
entries.followup_en: This was classic machine learning at Al Najat, not an LLM. The model looked good because it had seen the future. After I fixed the pipeline and used a time-based split, the score dropped, which was the honest number. Now a high test score makes me suspicious until I know how the data was split. That habit still helps me when people show me a shiny demo metric.
entries.answer_ar: في الإنذار المبكر كان التقييم وهمي بسبب تسريب البيانات، فتعلمت أحترم ترتيب الزمن داخل الـ Pipeline.

entries.answer_en: In question generation, a colleague wanted the system to publish questions by itself to save time. I wanted a teacher to approve every question. I asked what worried him, and it was speed. We measured a short review, not a full rewrite. We kept approval, and it was still much faster.
entries.followup_en: The generation pipeline retrieves unit content, writes questions from it, and stores a structured result. Production orchestration is Python, with a teacher approval step before save. Auto-publish would have been faster on paper, but a bad question in an exam is worse than a short review. Once we timed the review, the speed concern went away. I try to solve the real worry, not win the argument.
entries.answer_ar: زميلي أراد النشر التلقائي للأسئلة، واتفقنا على موافقة المعلم بعدما تأكدنا أن المراجعة سريعة.

entries.answer_en: Yes. Early in the BTEC work, there was pressure to send data to an outside model. I agreed we needed speed, but not with sending student data. I suggested curriculum text only, hide names, and one internal interface for model calls. Management accepted it, so we can change the model later without a rewrite.
entries.followup_en: I did not say no and stop. I offered a path that still showed results. We classify content first, send only curriculum material, and keep student identifiers out. All model calls go through one internal interface, so later we can move on-premise without rewriting the product. I presented it as a risk choice with an alternative. That is usually easier for a manager to accept than a hard block.
entries.answer_ar: لم أوافق على إرسال بيانات الطلاب لنموذج خارجي، واقترحت مساراً أسرع وآمناً عبر واجهة داخلية.

entries.answer_en: Payment systems taught me that pressure is normal and panic is optional. I make the scope clear, so we agree what must ship and what can wait. I protect testing, because skipping it creates a bigger problem later. And I speak early. A manager prefers a risk on Monday to a surprise on Friday.
entries.followup_en: In ministry payment work, a missed date was bad, but a wrong payment was worse. So I cut scope before I cut testing. I write down what is in and what is out, then I protect user acceptance. If a new request arrives mid-week, I say what will slip. Silence under pressure is what creates Friday emergencies. I would rather look cautious than look surprised.
entries.answer_ar: تحت الضغط أحدد النطاق بوضوح، ولا أضحّي بالاختبار، وأخبر المدير بالمخاطر مبكراً.

Teachers know what a fair result looks like. IT knows what can actually run. My job is to keep those two views in the same design. I do not disappear into code and come back with a surprise.

entries.answer_en: I learn by building. When RAG became important, I did not only read. I built the question generation pipeline and hit real problems, like state tracking and teacher approval. I follow official docs and test claims on my own data. Lately I have been studying evaluation, because measuring quality is where many teams are weak.
entries.followup_en: I read LangChain and LangGraph docs to understand the ideas, but production orchestration for question generation is Python, not LangGraph. Chroma was a prototype, not the production store. Recently I have been going deeper on faithfulness checks and RAGAS-style metrics. I have not run RAGAS as a production gate. I test claims on our own data before I trust a blog post. That keeps me current without collecting tools I cannot support.
entries.answer_ar: أتعلم بالبناء على بيانات حقيقية، ومؤخراً أركز على قياس جودة الإجابات لا على جمع أدوات جديدة.

entries.answer_en: I prioritize by impact and risk. Anything that touches production stability or data safety comes first, then whatever unblocks other people. Features come after that, ordered by value to users. I keep the list visible, and I renegotiate openly when something new arrives. That is the project manager in me.
entries.followup_en: If a model might leak student data, that jumps the queue over a nicer screen. If a tester is blocked, that jumps a nice-to-have feature. I learned this on payment projects: silent slipping is worse than a hard conversation. When a new request arrives, I say what will move down. People can accept a delay they can see. They cannot accept a surprise miss.
entries.answer_ar: أولويتي للسلامة واستقرار الإنتاج، ثم ما يفك حظر الآخرين، ثم الميزات حسب فائدتها.

entries.answer_en: I treat feedback like a test result, not an attack. Teachers told me the similarity checker gave too many false alarms. That was hard to hear, but useful. I tuned the threshold with them on real cases and showed evidence side by side. I would rather hear the problem than watch people stop using it.
entries.followup_en: False alarms were a trust problem, not only a metric problem. If teachers see too many flags, they ignore the tool. We sat with real assignments, moved the threshold, and changed the screen so both passages were visible. After that, they used it. I ask for the example, not the feeling. An example I can fix. A vague complaint I cannot.
entries.answer_ar: أتعامل مع النقد كمعلومة. المعلمون قالوا إن الإنذارات كثيرة، وعدّلت الحد معهم على حالات حقيقية.

entries.answer_en: I start from their question, not from the technology. A teacher does not care about embeddings. She cares if the tool is fair. So I say: it finds similar passages, shows them to you, and you decide. I show the real output, and I am honest about what the system cannot do.
entries.followup_en: Years as a project manager with ministry users taught me that trust comes from a clear sentence, not from impressive words. I use one picture or one real example, then I stop. If I say the model might guess, I say that in the first minute. Hiding limits is how people lose faith later. For finance leaders I would do the same: where the data goes, who approves, and what the log can prove.

entries.answer_en: I turn a vague request into a small example. For completion risk, people said find schools at risk. I asked: what does complete mean, on what date, and what should the output look like? We agreed on a definition, ten sample schools, and a one-page output. Then the design was clear.
entries.followup_en: That project was SQL, Pandas, and sklearn where the history supported it. No LLM. The word risk meant different things to different people. A sample of ten schools forced a decision: which date, which status, which columns on the page. After that, building was straightforward. I still do this with AI work. If we cannot show one good output, we are not ready to talk about architecture.
entries.answer_ar: أحوّل الطلب الغامض إلى مثال صغير: تعريف، عشر حالات، وصفحة واحدة، وبعدها يصبح التصميم واضحاً.

entries.followup_en: A demo that impresses a meeting does not motivate me for long. A tool that a teacher still uses next month does. I can move fast on a prototype, but I do not enjoy a culture that hides problems to look quick. I work well alone on a technical piece, and I work well in a team when the interfaces are clear. entries.answer_en: First month I listen and map: where data lives, how sensitive it is, and who the users are. Second month I pick one useful, lower-risk case, usually document questions with sources, and a small test set. Third month I harden it: checks, human approval, logs, and a model behind one interface.
entries.followup_en: I would not start by training a new model. I would start by reading access rules and talking to the people who own the documents. A first use case should be question answering with citations, because it is useful and easier to judge than full automation. The test set comes before the demo. In month three the interface matters, because it lets us move to an in-country model later without a rewrite. Small, measured, and safe.
entries.answer_ar: أول شهر أفهم البيانات والمستخدمين، ثاني شهر نموذج أسئلة مع مصادر واختبار، ثالث شهر أحصّنه بموافقة بشرية وسجلات.

listen_for: AI for a ministry of finance
entries.answer_en: You are a government financial organization, so the first question is where the data goes, not which model is smartest. Budget and salary data cannot leave the country, so in-country models come first. The value is answering from your own documents with sources, faster reporting, and a person approving anything that affects money.
entries.followup_en: I am not going to pretend I know internal systems I have not seen. What I do know is the constraint: finance data is sensitive, and a wrong automated action is expensive. That is close to payment systems and to the Ministry work I already do. Retrieval with citations is a better first bet than an agent that acts alone. I would want to learn your document stores and approval paths before I talk about tools.
entries.answer_ar: أنتم جهة مالية حكومية، فالسؤال الأول أين تذهب البيانات، والقيمة في إجابات من وثائقكم مع مصدر وموافقة بشرية.

entries.answer_en: Stop the damage first, then understand, then fix. Stopping means turn the feature off, roll back, or use a fallback. Then I read the logs and reconstruct what happened, because in finance you must say exactly what the system did. Then I fix the cause and add a test so it cannot return quietly.
entries.followup_en: That order comes from payment systems. A rushed patch under pressure can be worse than a short outage. I tell the owner what users see, what we switched off, and when the next update will come. After the fix, I want a test that would have caught it, and a log that an auditor can read. For AI, the same pattern: if answers go wrong, disable the path, do not keep serving guesses while we investigate.

aliases: how do you think about responsible ai

entries.answer_en: For me it is practical, not a speech. The system should show its source, say I do not know instead of guessing, and keep personal data inside the organization. A person must approve anything that affects a person or money. In my BTEC work, the similarity checker showed evidence, and a teacher decided.
entries.followup_en: Fairness for me is also about false alarms. If a tool flags too many students, it is not fair, even if the model is clever. Privacy means we do not send student identifiers to an outside model. Logging means we can reconstruct a decision later. I do not treat responsible AI as a poster on the wall. It is design choices: sources, refusal, approval, and a small data footprint.
entries.answer_ar: الذكاء الاصطناعي المسؤول عندي عملي: مصدر، وما يخمن، وبيانات داخل الجهة، وشخص يوافق على أي قرار يمس الناس أو المال.

entries.answer_en: Making teachers trust an AI tool that touches student assessment. The technical part of the similarity checker was manageable. The hard part was trust: a tool that accuses students gets rejected. I changed the design, not the model. The system flags, shows both passages, and the teacher decides.
entries.followup_en: Embeddings and cosine similarity were the easy layer. The hard layer was false alarms and fairness. We sat with teachers on real cases and moved the threshold until the list was usable. We also refused to let the tool issue a verdict. In sensitive domains, the human boundary is the product. That lesson is why I still push for approval steps in question generation, even when someone wants full automation.

entries.answer_en: It is the first technology in my career that can read language and help people directly, not only move data around. When I built the voice kiosk and saw people talk to a machine and get help, I knew this was the direction. Making these systems safe is as interesting as making them work.
entries.followup_en: I did not start in generative AI. I started in payments, then applied machine learning at Al Najat: the Whisper kiosk, early-warning, and helpdesk classification. The kiosk was speech to text and a flow, not an LLM. The Ministry work from 2023 is where RAG and generation began. I moved into AI because users could finally talk and read with the system. I stayed because the safety problems are real, and I like solving them.

entries.question: How do you mentor a junior engineer or review their code?
aliases: how do you mentor a junior engineer
how do you review someone else code
what do you look for in a code review
how do you bring a new engineer up to speed
how do you give technical feedback to a colleague
entries.answer_en: I start by asking what the code is supposed to guarantee, because most review comments are really disagreements about the requirement. Then I separate three things: something that is wrong, something that is risky, and something I would write differently. Only the first two block. The third is an opinion and I say so.
entries.followup_en: With a junior I explain what breaks, instead of handing over the fix. I also ask for a test that fails before the change. Fifteen years taught me that the expensive bugs are the ones nobody can repeat. So I push for logs and clear steps more than for style. I also say when I am not sure. A reviewer who is always certain teaches people to hide problems.
entries.answer_ar: أبدأ بسؤال ما الذي يفترض أن يضمنه هذا الكود، لأن أغلب ملاحظات المراجعة هي في الحقيقة خلاف على المتطلب. ثم أفصل ثلاثة أشياء: ما هو خطأ، وما هو خطِر، وما كنت سأكتبه بشكل مختلف. الأولان فقط يوقفان الدمج. والثالث رأي وأقول ذلك صراحة.
